Survival along a record of temperature, from a fitted failure-rate model

Source: R/predict-survival.R
predict_survival.Rd

Predicts, from a model fitted with fit_hazard(), the survival of an individual exposed to a measured record of temperature: the probability of surviving to each time of the record and of failing by its end, each with its posterior median and credible interval, at the covariate values in each row of newdata. Random effects are set to zero, so the prediction is for a typical group.

Usage

predict_survival(
  fit,
  record,
  newdata = NULL,
  levels = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  prob = 0.95,
  n_draws = 1000,
  grid_dT = 0.1
)

Arguments

fit

A brmsfit, a model fitted with fit_hazard().

record

A data frame with the columns time and temp, the record of temperature through time, in the time unit and temperature scale of the data the model was fitted to, with times increasing and no gaps. It may also hold the column of a co-stressor and the column named in by.

newdata

A data frame with one row per set of covariate values to predict at, holding every covariate in the parameters' formulas. NULL (the default) suits a model with no covariates.

levels

A named numeric vector giving the level of each co-stressor that record does not follow, on its measurement scale, e.g. c(DO = 6).

by

A character string, the name of a column of record giving the period each reading belongs to (e.g., a day). When given, the result has each period's share of the hazard accrued over the record. An interval between two readings belongs to the period of the first.

prob

A single number between 0 and 1, the coverage of the credible intervals. Defaults to 0.95.

n_draws

A single number, the number of posterior draws to use, evenly spaced through the posterior. Defaults to 1000. The draws are held for every step along the record, so a long record with many draws needs memory in proportion to their product.

grid_dT

A single positive number, the largest change in temperature within a step along the record, in degrees. Between two readings the temperature is taken to change linearly, and the hazard is accrued in steps over which it changes by at most this much, since the failure rate at the midpoint of a step stands for the whole of it (see The time grid in build_hazard_data). Defaults to 0.1; Inf takes one step between consecutive readings.

Value

A list of tibbles, each with the columns of newdata:

  • survival: for each time of the record, the posterior mean, median, lower and upper of the probability of surviving to it (1 at the first time).

  • mortality: the same for the probability of failing by the end of the record.

  • risk (when by is given): each period's share of the hazard accrued over the record. The shares of a posterior draw add to one; n_draws is the number of draws with any hazard, which the summary rests on.

  • coverage: the lowest and highest temperatures at which failures were observed in the data (Ta_failed_min, Ta_failed_max); the share of the record's duration below, within and above them; the share of the hazard accrued along the record at those temperatures (risk_below, risk_within, risk_above); the longest exposure in the data (tau_max); and the share of the record's duration that comes after it (beyond) with the share of the hazard accrued there (risk_beyond). Each share of the hazard is the median over the posterior draws with any hazard.

  • record: the times and temperatures of the record, with any co-stressor it follows, kept so that plot_survival() can draw them above the survival they led to.

Details

Along the record the cumulative hazard grows, over each step, by M(T) (H0(tau_1) - H0(tau_0)): the failure rate at the temperature in the middle of the step, times the growth of the cumulative baseline hazard over it. A step is the interval between two readings, or a part of it where the temperature changes by more than grid_dT between them. Survival to a time is exp(-cumulative hazard up to it). With the memoryless baseline the growth of H0 is the length of the interval, so the cumulative hazard is the failure rate summed over the record, and it does not matter where the record begins. With the other baselines the hazard depends on elapsed exposure, which is counted from the first time in the record.

Outside the temperatures and exposures of the assay

An assay is run at temperatures that cause failure within its duration, and a field record may lie below them. At the temperatures at which failures were observed the data hold the failure-rate function in place, so functions that fit equally well predict alike. Below them nothing does, and the prediction depends on which function was chosen: functions that fit the assay equally well can differ by orders of magnitude there. The temperatures that count are those at which individuals failed, and not all those they were exposed to. In a ramping assay every individual starts at a temperature at which none fails, and the time spent there shows only that failures were rare over that time.

The coverage table gives the share of the record below, within and above the temperatures at which failures were observed, by duration and by the risk accrued. The second is the one to read: a record may spend most of its time at cool temperatures where little hazard accrues, and take nearly all of its risk from a few warm hours that the assay did cover.

A record may also last longer than any exposure in the assay. With a baseline other than the memoryless one, the prediction then rests on how the baseline extends beyond the exposures the data hold, and with the memoryless one on the assumption that the hazard does not change with the time under exposure, which the data support only over those exposures. The coverage table also gives the longest exposure in the data and the share of the record, by duration and by the risk accrued, that comes after it.

A message is given when any of the record lies outside the temperatures or after the longest exposure. Comparing the predictions of several failure-rate functions and baselines, or averaging them with average_survival(), shows how much the prediction depends on those choices.

The zero-type failure rates (zeroexp, zeropower) are zero at the reference temperature Tr and are taken as zero below it. The power function is not defined below Tr, and a record that goes below it is refused.

The mean and the median

Each posterior draw gives a probability of surviving, and the tables summarise those probabilities by their mean and by their median. The mean is the probability of surviving with the uncertainty in the parameters taken into account (and, from average_survival(), the uncertainty about the model, as far as the weights measure it): it is the fraction of individuals expected to survive in a typical group (random effects at zero). The median is the value that half of the posterior lies below. The two are close when the posterior is concentrated, and differ when it is skewed or has two separate groups of values, as it can when models that disagree are averaged; the credible interval should then be reported with either.

No recovery

The hazard accrued along the record is only ever added to, so the prediction assumes that an individual does not recover when the temperature returns to a range in which repair is expected to exceed thermal damage. Along a record that moves in and out of stressful temperatures, such as one with a daily cycle, the predicted mortality is then too high if individuals recover in between, and the more so the more cycles there are.

Co-stressors

For a model with co-stressors, a co-stressor whose column is in record is followed through time, taking in each interval the value halfway between the two readings. One that is not in record is held at the level given in levels.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# a model fitted to a small ramping trial: 20 individuals warmed from 20 to 35
# degrees over 60 minutes and checked every 10, in two trials (see fit_hazard())
path   <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = c(0, 60), temp = c(20, 35))
checks <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = seq(0, 60, by = 10))
ind    <- data.frame(id = 1:20, path_id = "A", event = 1, mass = runif(20, 8, 12),
                     trial = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 10),
                     t_upper = sample(seq(10, 60, 10), 20, replace = TRUE))
long   <- build_hazard_data(ind, path, "interval", covariates = c("mass", "trial"),
                            checks = checks)
fit    <- fit_hazard(long, "exp", dpar_formulas = list(loga = ~ 1 + mass))

pred <- predict_survival(fit, record, newdata = data.frame(mass = 10), by = "day")
pred$mortality
pred$risk
} # }
